# Voice profile — eff-mullin

## 1. Cadence

Sentences run at medium length while building a legal or policy argument, then snap short when the verdict lands — 9/11 samples. The pattern is reproducible: let the explanation fill two or three clauses, then close the paragraph with a sentence half as long. In `californias-ab-412-still-demands-developers-do-impossible`: *"That may seem straightforward. In practice, it's anything but."* In `why-are-gay-bars-building-databases-their-patrons`, after three descriptive sentences: *"This was not simply checking IDs at the door. PatronScan was building a database."* In `kids-online-safety-act-will-make-internet-worse-everyone`, the same verdict sentence appears twice in the piece, once to open a section and once to close it — the only instance of deliberate repetition in the corpus. The short sentence is the claim; the longer sentences before it are the mechanism. Write the mechanism, then cut to the claim.

Contractions run throughout all 11 samples — counted as [measurement:contractions] Count whole-word n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, and 'm forms plus 's only for the closed elision hosts it, that, there, here, who, what, where, when, how, why, he, she, let, one, nothing, everything, something, somebody, nobody, and this; possessive 's is excluded — 86 instances, 10.66 per 1,000 words, throughout. Against them sit 32 uncontracted negatives in 9/11 samples, counted as [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] Count case-insensitive whole phrases do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, and had not in the extracted sample bodies — 3.97 per 1,000 words, several times per piece. The uncontracted form appears in the same paragraphs as contractions; its function is emphasis. *"There is no machine-readable 'list'"* lands harder than *"there's no machine-readable 'list'."* Use the uncontracted form when the negation is the point.

Parenthetical spans are pervasive across all 11 samples — counted as [measurement:round-parenthetical-spans] Count each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line in the extracted sample bodies — 97 instances, 12.03 per 1,000 words, throughout. They carry bill citations, cross-references, and factual qualifications without breaking the sentence's forward motion. Em-dashes appear in 10/11 samples — counted as [measurement:em-dashes] Count every literal em-dash character in the extracted sample bodies — 53 instances, 6.57 per 1,000 words, several times per piece — and serve a sharper interruption: inserting a phrase that reframes what just came before, as in *"a cumbersome beast at best—neither machine-readable nor accessible"* (`californias-ab-412-bill`).

## 2. How a piece opens

Three opening shapes appear across 11/11 samples. Most common (6/11): name the legislation in the first sentence and frame EFF's position within two sentences — `kids-online-safety-act-will-make-internet-worse-everyone`: *"The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA) is back in the Senate. Sponsors are claiming—again—that the latest version won't censor online content. It isn't true."* Second (2/11): an urgent news hook — a vote just happened or is days away — names the legislation as an event: `congress-just-rushed-through-disastrous-copyright-office-overhaul` opens on *"In a voice vote earlier this week."* Third (3/11): a principle or scene precedes the legislation — `court-records-should-be-free` begins *"Court records belong to the public"*; `why-are-gay-bars-building-databases-their-patrons` begins with *"Recent reports have raised alarm."* All three shapes reach the bill and EFF's position within the first three sentences. No piece withholds its argument past the opening paragraph.

## 3. How a piece closes

Eight of 11 samples end on a short directive sentence naming what Congress, the Senate, or a specific institution should do: `congress-just-rushed`: *"The Senate should reject H.R. 6028. The Copyright Office should serve the public—not presidential administrations, and not industry lobbyists."*; `kids-online-safety`: *"Lawmakers should reject it, and fast."*; `why-are-gay-bars`: *"These businesses should reject PatronScan."* Two pieces close with coalition citations or a prompt to read a full letter (`court-records`, `no-fakes`). Three pieces within the AB-412 thread close with a California-resident action call. The closing sentence in almost every case is shorter than the final paragraph above it.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The pronoun carrying the argument is *we*, meaning EFF as an organization — counted as [measurement:first-person-plural-family] Count case-sensitive whole-word tokens we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours, and the listed contracted we forms in the extracted sample bodies; uppercase US is excluded — 19 instances, 10/11 samples, 2.36 per 1,000 words, once or twice per piece. This is institutional, not inclusive: *"EFF has used this process repeatedly"*, *"we continue to believe A.B. 412 is simply unworkable."* It does not draw the reader into a shared *we*; it positions EFF as actor and narrator simultaneously.

First-person singular does not appear in 9/11 samples at all; the 2 samples that contain it have one instance each — counted as [measurement:first-person-singular-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens I, me, my, mine, and myself in the extracted sample bodies — 2 instances total, 0.25 per 1,000 words. The author does not appear as an individual with views. Never write *I believe*; write *EFF believes* or *we oppose*.

Second person (*you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, you'll*) appears in 5/11 samples — counted as [measurement:second-person-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, and you'll in the extracted sample bodies — 11 instances, 1.36 per 1,000 words, once or twice per piece where it appears. It is used almost exclusively for action calls: *"If you are a California resident and want to speak out..."* It does not appear in the analytical paragraphs. When making the argument, actors are named in third person — companies, lawmakers, platforms. Reserve *you* for explicit reader action calls.

Questions are sparse: 9 question marks across 4/11 samples, counted as [measurement:question-marks] Count every literal question-mark character in the extracted sample bodies — 1.12 per 1,000 words, once or twice per piece where they appear. When questions appear, they name the problem a bill fails to answer and are followed immediately by an answer in the next sentence.

Named actors appear throughout 11/11 samples: bills by full name and number, companies by name, court cases by citation, coalition partners listed by organization. The argument is always grounded in specific legislative text or named precedent, never attributed to an unnamed "some argue" formulation — 11/11 samples, throughout.

## 5. Figures

Figures appear in 9/11 samples but are deployed one at a time and never extended. Each figure occupies one clause; the next sentence is plain. The vocabulary is drawn from legal procedure, economics, and conjuring: *"a heckler's veto"* (`no-fakes-act`), *"legislative sleight-of-hand"* (`kids-online-safety`), *"a death sentence"* for a startup, *"a cumbersome beast"* (`californias-ab-412-bill`), *"weaponize copyright claims"* (`california-ab-412-stalls-out`), *"a solution in search of a problem"* (`californias-ab-412-still`), *"a smokescreen"* (`kids-online-safety`). Use the figure once and do not develop it. No figure in the corpus runs beyond the clause that introduces it and none reappears in a later paragraph. No rate is given: no reproducible rule can reliably bound a figurative phrase across readers.

## 6. Register range

The register stays in policy advocacy across all 11 samples. Variation is in stance rather than vocabulary: pieces opposing legislation argue through consequences systematically; pieces supporting legislation are shorter and more affirmatory (`court-records-should-be-free`, 360 words). `why-are-gay-bars-building-databases-their-patrons` shifts toward investigative mode — it quotes legislative analyses, cites specific figures from bill hearings, and narrates a documented history — but the advocacy frame and directive close are present throughout. The institutional *we*, the sentence-then-verdict rhythm, and the named-actor argument do not shift by topic, length, or legislative direction.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Profanity is absent across all 11 samples — counted as [measurement:profanity-vulgarity] Count only the case-insensitive whole-word profanity and vulgarity forms enumerated by the prose-author corpus-rates profanity rule; coined words containing a rude root are excluded — 0 instances, 0 per 1,000 words, establishing the absence across 11/11. The weight carried elsewhere by shock or intensity is carried here by specific figures: penalty amounts (*"$250,000 per violation"*), named companies, precise statutory language. Name the number; quote the statute; name the company. That specificity does the work.

Extended metaphors do not appear in any sample — 11/11 establish this. The positive habit is elaborated legal argument: when the writing wants to make a problem feel large, it piles on statutory consequences across sentences rather than developing a comparison. Write the figure once (section 5); then build the case in plain policy language.

First-person singular is effectively absent — 9/11 samples have none at all, 0.25 per 1,000 words across the corpus — against 19 instances of the institutional first-person plural at 2.36 per 1,000 words in 10/11 samples. The *we* occupies the space where an authorial *I* would otherwise stand. Both sides of this pair are measured in section 4.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

No voice card was provided; all observations are derived from the corpus alone.

All 11 samples are advocacy posts about specific pieces of legislation. The corpus does not show how the voice behaves in a register without a legislative target — a purely explanatory post, an event recap, or a piece that is primarily celebratory rather than argumentative.

Sub-headings appear inside 9/11 pieces. Whether this structural choice belongs to the author or to EFF's CMS and editorial process is not determinable from this corpus; no observation about heading use is made.

4 observations were considered and dropped: sentence-initial *But* as a stylistic marker — present but not consistently distinctive across samples; ironic framing of opponents' positions — clear in 1/11, not a pattern; deliberate sentence repetition for rhetorical emphasis — 1/11 (`kids-online-safety`); the *not just X, but Y* construction — present in several samples but not frequent or distinct enough to rate or describe reliably.
